name: Sen. Jacky Rosen
subject: Why I'm leading the charge in the Senate to combat antisemitism
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Rosen for Nevada
body:
We must stop the epidemic of antisemitic violence and harassment.
| | |
---
Friend,
I am the third Jewish woman and the first former synagogue president ever elected to the United States Senate. Think about that: In our nation’s 250-year history, there were only TWO Jewish women elected to the Senate before I joined.
Like any believer, my faith is deeply tied to who I am, what I fight for, and my role as a lawmaker. It’s part of why I care about the issues that I do, and it means that I bring with me the same struggles that all Jews face. Most prominently, the threat and impact of antisemitism.
**That's why I'm leading the charge in the Senate to combat the increasing levels of violence and harassment Jewish Americans are facing right now.**
[**_Will you please make a gift of $5 or more to support my work in Washington to fight the epidemic of antisemitism across our country?_**](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/136567054/637866201/910177728?amounts=250,100,50,25,5&amount=5&refcode=jtk5868-fr-nd&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNDAvMS84ODI5OCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICI4MDQ4NmIyMi05ODhmLWYxMTEtYjMzNy0wMDBkM2ExNTU4Y2UiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=sAWnbbIxALoSDsWlpMFc_Gh2IBav2a5zob42gWIQRCw=)
| | [Donate $5](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/136567055/637866294/1781803786?amounts=250,100,50,25,5&amount=5&refcode=jtk5868-fr-nd&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNDAvMS84ODI5OCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICI4MDQ4NmIyMi05ODhmLWYxMTEtYjMzNy0wMDBkM2ExNTU4Y2UiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=sAWnbbIxALoSDsWlpMFc_Gh2IBav2a5zob42gWIQRCw=)
---
For me, this fight is personal. When I was just a few years old, I was playing in a hotel swimming pool with my mom while on vacation when a lifeguard on duty told her that we were “dirty” because we were Jewish – and that we had to leave the pool immediately because of it. My parents packed up our things and left that hotel. We never returned. My mom never forgot that interaction, retelling the story for years.
[](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/136567056/637866332/1781803786?amounts=250,100,50,25,5&refcode=jtk5868-fr-nd&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNDAvMS84ODI5OCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICI4MDQ4NmIyMi05ODhmLWYxMTEtYjMzNy0wMDBkM2ExNTU4Y2UiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=sAWnbbIxALoSDsWlpMFc_Gh2IBav2a5zob42gWIQRCw=)
Nearly every Jewish American has a moment in their lives when they experience or witness antisemitism like that firsthand, and the problem is especially serious today.
Swastika graffiti. Physical assaults and threats. Firebombings. **Multiple** deadly mass shootings. These attacks on Jews are not isolated incidents. They represent a regression toward one of civilization’s darkest chapters.

disclaimer_text: Paid for by Chris Pappas for Senate
body:
This is a coordinated strategy to intimidate voters and tilt the midterms to the GOP.
Hi there, it's Marc Elias.
I’ll get right to the point: We have less than 100 days until the midterm elections, **[and I’m asking you to split a donation of $5 between Chris Pappas’s campaign and the DSCC to help flip the Senate blue.](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260803_2.5_Qutq&refcode=em20260803-2&t=1&akid=8107%2E582294%2E8VCu_D)**
Here is why your support right now is so critical:
* Republicans view New Hampshire as one of their best opportunities to flip a Senate seat.
* GOP super PACs and dark money groups are pledging millions to back Chris’s opponent John Sununu and move the Granite State backward.
* MAGA billionaires are determined to buy this open Senate seat and notch another rubber stamp for Donald Trump’s reckless agenda.

We just won a massive victory in court striking down New Hampshire's unconstitutional HB 1569 voter suppression law – but now Trump’s DOJ is deploying federal "election monitors" directly into Manchester and Nashua, demanding access to private state voter records, and threatening local election officials.
Make no mistake: This isn’t about election integrity. It’s a coordinated strategy to intimidate voters and tilt the midterms in the GOP’s favor.
**I spend my days fighting these unconstitutional attacks in court, but litigation alone won't protect this seat. We need a pro-democracy firewall in the Senate, and that starts with electing Chris Pappas.**
**[Before our crucial fundraising deadline, will you split $5 or more between Chris Pappas and the DSCC to elect candidates who will fight back against voter suppression and help flip the Senate blue?](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260803_2.5_Qutq&refcode=em20260803-2&t=2&akid=8107%2E582294%2E8VCu_D)**

The GOP is counting on exhaustion and resignation to win this election. We cannot – and will not – give them either.
Thank you for standing up for our democracy,
Marc Elias

name: Abdul El-Sayed
subject: What’s going through my mind
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Abdul for U
body:
Peter,
Tomorrow, Michiganders decide who wins this competitive primary. I wanted to write to you myself and share what’s going through my mind heading into one of the most important days of my life.
Corporate billionaires, AIPAC, and Trump-aligned mega donors have poured more than $61 million into ads stretching the truth about me. They're doing it because they know my opponent will keep doing their bidding in Washington, and I won't.
**This campaign was never about pleasing the people who write those checks.** It's about taking on the powerful, and building something different: lower costs, Medicare for All, and money out of politics for good.
That's why Bernie Sanders stood with us. It's why the UAW stood with us. AOC. Leaders across this state, from Detroit to the U.P.
Tomorrow is the day we find out if it was enough. I believe it can be — but only if we all show up.
**Thank you for every bit of trust you've placed in me.** Whatever happens tomorrow, I'm grateful for it.
And Peter, if you have anything left to give tonight, it would mean the world:
[**https://secure.actblue.com/donate/em-ms-aes-20260803-3-ak**](https://act.abdulformichigan.com/go/507?c0=em-ms-aes-20260803-3-ak.gx1MLn&amount=5&refcode=em20260803-2816&t=3&akid=2821%2E251025%2EQaT2Pi)
Let’s go win this,
Abdul

Hey, folks – it’s Sherrod Brown.
Right now, I’m 3 points down in the polls, and the GOP’s attacks are ramping up by the day. That’s because our race here in Ohio will decide Senate control.
I’m running a grassroots campaign, so with experts predicting that this will be the most expensive U.S. Senate race in history, I can’t win without you. If you’re able to chip in $5 or just a few bucks today to power our fight, I’d really appreciate it.
Here’s the link to donate: **_[https://secure.actblue.com/donate/sherrod-email-q3-2026](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/136567591/637891393/-1664069836?amounts=250,100,50,25,5&amount=5&refcode=jtk5706-fr-t1nd&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMTMvMS84NzY0NSIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICI3OGFhMmQ2OC05ZThmLWYxMTEtYjMzNy0wMDBkM2ExNTU4Y2UiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=sL2s8JLxw9GFBVT5WMLJmgQQiUVqhD4nZuCiavyoDoE=)_**
My decision to run for the Senate wasn’t made lightly.
I love Ohio. I’m biased, of course, but I think we have the greatest, most hardworking people in the world. Throughout my time in public service, I’ve fought to improve the lives of everyday Ohioans and ensure that working folks get their fair share.
**I also love this country – and when you love your country, you fight for the people who make it work.**
That’s why it’s so upsetting to see how politicians in Washington have turned their backs on working people. Politicians like Jon Husted, my opponent in this race.
Husted says he’s fighting for Ohioans, but instead, he’s catered to his billionaire donors and corporate interest allies from the moment he stepped foot in the U.S. Senate. He’s ripped away health care from working people to fund the largest tax break for billionaires in American history, and he’s failed to take a stand against the Trump administration when Ohioans are being harmed.
I never planned to run for office again after 2024, but seeing all of this chaos, corruption, and self-dealing coming out of Washington, I knew I had to get back in the fight.
And I’m so glad I did.
Ever since launching this campaign, hundreds of thousands of folks like you have joined our grassroots movement for change, and we’re making incredible progress to win this race.
**But we’re in for a tough final few months: Republicans are spending $133 million to defeat me and save their Senate majority, and this surge of money is causing a dip in our momentum.**
We can fight back, but just as in elections past, I can’t do it alone.

body:
Thank you for helping me write this love letter to Michigan

| |
---|---|---

# [A personal message the night before the primary](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=6380051&post_id=209673922&utm_source=post-email-title&utm_campaign=email-post-title&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjA5NjczOTIyLCJpYXQiOjE3ODU4MDU0MTksImV4cCI6MTc4ODM5NzQxOSwiaXNzIjoicHViLTYzODAwNTEiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.Er-zSwGinhVHOtjd44vwSzl6YEyGjZd39GqpUERlCUc)
### Thank you for helping me write this love letter to Michigan
| | [Haley Stevens](https://substack.com/@haleyformi)
---
| Aug 3
---
| [](https://substack.com/@haleyformi)
---

---
| | | [](https://open.substack.com/pub/haleyformi/p/a-personal-message-the-night-before?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=email-restack-comment&action=restack-comment&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjA5NjczOTIyLCJpYXQiOjE3ODU4MDU0MTksImV4cCI6MTc4ODM5NzQxOSwiaXNzIjoicHViLTYzODAwNTEiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.Er-zSwGinhVHOtjd44vwSzl6YEyGjZd39GqpUERlCUc&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email)
---
| | [READ IN APP](https://open.substack.com/pub/haleyformi/p/a-personal-message-the-night-before?utm_source=email&redirect=app-store&utm_campaign=email-read-in-app)
---

Here we are, friends.
Tomorrow, Michiganders will vote in the primary to decide which Democrat will face Mike Rogers in November.
There's nothing left for me to say that I haven't already said in a union hall or on somebody's porch.
**What I keep thinking about is the people I 'm in this for.** I've met a lot of Michiganders during this campaign, and I mean it when I say I'm carrying each of you around with me. I see your faces, I think about what you said, I remember your stories.
I'll meet somebody and chat with them for a few minutes at a diner, and then six months later I'm in a committee hearing in Washington, and their face turns up in my head. And it reminds me what's important - the real folks behind the policies.
I've got a lot of those faces in my head now.
I think about Myleka behind the counter at her bagel place in Grand Rapids, the apprentices at the UA Local 85 picnic, the little girl who flexed for our camera like Rosie the Riveter, the woman who runs the pet store in South Haven, the gals at the fish fry on Tigers Opening Day who came up to me in tears worried about their energy bill, the mom on a porch in Detroit who asked plainly what I was going to do about her rising insurance premium ... all of these good folks who deserve a fighter in the Senate.
That's who this is for. These Michiganders are the reason I'm doing this.
I'm proud that we ran this campaign the way Michiganders actually live. We showed up in small rooms in every corner of this state and we listened, we learned, and then we told people directly what we'd do and why.
That's it. That's the whole strategy. It's not glamorous, but public service rarely is.
**The most exciting part is that if we win, I get to keep doing this good, hard work.** Lowering costs. Protecting Social Security and health care. Bringing manufacturing home. Standing up to Donald Trump and Mike Rogers. Being the person in that room who is thinking about the mom on the porch in Detroit while the other side is thinking about their right-wing MAGA billionaire donors.
I have fought for Michigan my entire life. **I love this state. It made me who I am - a gritty policy geek with a special place in her heart for the place that raised her.**
And tomorrow, it's up to Michigan to decide who represents them in the U.S. Senate. That's exactly how it's supposed to be. That's the whole point of the thing. Michigan voters decide. I love that about this country, even on the nights it makes me a little anxious.
So I'm asking one favor tonight:
Please, make a plan to vote tomorrow. Polls are open from 7 a.m. until 8 p.m. And if your absentee ballot is still at home, don't mail it at this point - hand-deliver it to your local clerk's office.
If you've already voted, thank you. Now I want you to be a little annoying: call your sister, text your neighbor, remind them tomorrow is the big day. We can't let up.
**[And if you 're able, chip in tonight to help us reach every last voter in the final hours.](https://substack.com/redirect/e6acffe8-2431-48ed-979a-5044545fb409?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
Last thing: THANK YOU.
I mean that. Thousands of you chipped in, knocked doors, made calls. You told me your stories. I'm honored to fight for you.
This whole campaign has been a love letter to Michigan. I'm grateful you've helped me write it.
With gratitude,
Haley

A personal note from Haley 👋

I'm a lifelong Michigander and the daughter of small-business owners. I've spent my career fighting for Michigan's working families - and now I'm running for the U.S. Senate to keep standing up for the people I love.

But here's the truth: Senate control could come down to Michigan. And Trump and his megadonors know it. That's why they're gearing up to spend tens of millions to defeat me and hand this seat to a MAGA Republican.

I need your help to fight back. This race will be one of the most competitive - and expensive - in the country, and I'm counting on grassroots support to win.

If you're with me, will you chip in today?
[Donate](https://substack.com/redirect/e6acffe8-2431-48ed-979a-5044545fb409?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

Zohran Mamdani is spending $70 million on five city-owned stores that undercut every bodega in the city. Glenn Beck did the math, and his line stuck with us: this isn't a fight between two grocers. It's a grocer against a grocer's tax collector.
Everybody assumes it collapses. Investor David Friedberg went on All-In and explained why it won't, at least not fast, and why that's so much worse.

He sat in front of a Senate committee last Wednesday and took the Fifth on all of it. Josh Hawley didn't let it go quietly, and how he finished is worth hearing.
Here's the part that's ours. In 2020, while Mark was running for Senate, an Albuquerque oncologist put on a white coat and cut an ad calling him anti-science for saying COVID came from a lab. He's still waiting on the correction.

A new poll has the governor's race tighter than expected, and Deb Haaland's campaign emailed supporters calling it "a tough one."
Mark's run this play himself. He tells you what that email is really doing, and the one thing to watch for that means the race is genuinely close. It hasn't happened yet.

Sophie Cunningham said women's sports should be for biological women, so two teenagers showed up courtside in Seattle with signs thanking her. A Storm co-owner walked over and cursed at them until one of them cried.
Five-game suspension. Mark asked the only question that matters.

| I've read this supposed "deal," and I want you to know exactly why its not worth the paper it is written on.
---
[](https://act.adamschiff.com/go/7929?t=6&amount=10&refcode=aschiff_email_080326_blanche&akid=10033%2E5257348%2EofcF4i)
Derek, The Republican holdouts on the Judiciary Committee are about to make Todd Blanche the next Attorney General of the United States. Their cover: two statements, one signed by Todd Blanche late Sunday night, and the other unsigned, that supposedly kill Trump's $1.8 billion slush fund and limit the IRS giveaway. **I've read this supposed "deal," Derek, and I want you to know exactly why it fails to meet the smell test:** It _doesn't_ prevent future payouts to the violent insurrectionists Trump pardoned for attacking police officers. It _doesn't_ prevent the administration from bringing the slush fund back from the dead next week, or from using the Justice Department's Judgment Fund for the same illicit purpose. _And_ it leaves in place a tax-immunity deal that could help Trump and his family avoid paying taxes on the $2.3 billion he made last year. It also merely expresses an interpretation of who the tax deal applies to — leaving Trump to challenge that interpretation in court. Todd Blanche says he stands by his testimony from before our committee last month. He pledged — under oath — to provide Congress with assistance on a bill to make the death of Donald Trump's slush fund enforceable by law. So what assistance has he provided in the month since he made that promise? No bill. No assistance. Nothing. Nada. These Judiciary Committee Republicans should not settle for anything less than the Acting Attorney General keeping his promise, and helping us write the death of this slush fund into law. And for the rest of us, no parsing of this sham settlement should be enough to overcome Blanche’s terrible leadership of DOJ. **I’ll keep fighting, but the way we kill this slush fund and IRS sham for good is to flip four seats, take back the Senate, and put people in charge who answer to you instead of Donald Trump.** **[Will you chip in $10 or whatever you can to help Democrats flip the Senate in November?](https://act.adamschiff.com/go/7929?t=12&amount=10&refcode=aschiff_email_080326_blanche&akid=10033%2E5257348%2EofcF4i)** _If you've saved your payment information with ActBlue Express, your donation will go through immediately:_ | | [DONATE $10→](https://act.adamschiff.com/go/7929?t=13&amount=10&express_lane=true&refcode=aschiff_email_080326_blanche&akid=10033%2E5257348%2EofcF4i)

subject: Trump doesn’t have the authority – so I’m taking him to court
disclaimer_text: PAID FOR BY ROB BONTA FOR CALIFORNIA ATTORNEY GENERAL 2026 FPPC ID #145642
body:
https://secure.actblue.com/donate/rb-email-26 [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/rb-email-26]
As a society, we should be judged by how we treat the most vulnerable among us. Across the board, Trump gets straight F's.
The latest example: The Trump administration is trying to raid the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program for the sensitive personal data of families who rely on it to get by.
TANF provides critical cash assistance to lower-income families across the country, including 350,000 families in California every single month . The program ensures children don’t go hungry and helps struggling families get by.
Recently, in a blatant and unlawful attempt to dramatically broaden their role in overseeing TANF, the Trump administration claimed it has the authority to share years' worth of TANF recipients’ most sensitive data. Social Security numbers, marital status, income data, and more — all of it they want to share with DHS and any other federal, state, or private entity it chooses.
Trump doesn’t have that authority. So today I filed our 81st lawsuit against the Trump administration in 80 weeks, leading a multistate coalition of 23 attorneys general and two governors to put a stop to this cruel, unnecessary, and illegal mass surveillance effort.
If this work is important to you, I’m personally asking you to help keep it going by making a donation today. Will you chip in any amount right now? [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/rb-email-26]
DONATE NOW [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/rb-email-26]
Congress designed TANF 30 years ago in a way that specifically limits federal overreach and gives states the flexibility and autonomy to run their own anti-poverty programs. This administration is attempting to seize power that Congress never gave it — in violation of the laws Congress passed and the spending clause of the Constitution.
This is part of a pattern. This administration has tried to share unfettered personal health data from HHS with DHS, seize information about millions of SNAP recipients, and is working on a mass surveillance effort using data from Americans who never consented to it. We’ve gone to court to stop it again and again — and we blocked both HHS’s attempt to share information with DHS and USDA’s demands for information about SNAP recipients.
People who are struggling shouldn't have to be afraid to turn to their government for help — to feed and clothe their kids, to keep a roof over their heads, or to get critical medical care. They shouldn't have to worry that accessing that help will result in the exploitation of their personal information.
I’m running for re-election to continue my fight to hold this administration accountable and protect Californians’ rights and freedoms. Will you make a contribution to help power this work today? Please give $25 today: [https://secure.actblue.com/donate/rb-email-26]

You have my word: I will never stop protecting Californians' personal and private data, and I’ll never stop pushing back against this president's mass surveillance efforts.
I will never stop defending the rule of law, and I will always stand up for those who have the least.

This administration has tried to share unfettered personal health data from HHS with DHS, seize information about millions of SNAP recipients, and is working on a mass surveillance effort using data from Americans who never consented to it. We’ve gone to court to stop it again and again — and we blocked both HHS’s attempt to share information with DHS and USDA’s demands for information about SNAP recipients. People who are struggling shouldn't have to be afraid to turn to their government for help — to feed and clothe their kids, to keep a roof over their heads, or to get critical medical care. They shouldn't have to worry that accessing that help will result in the exploitation of their personal information. **Fair businesses strengthen countries, helping the economy and everyone in it.**
**Unfair, highly exploitative, and predatory mega-businesses degrade and destroy the nation that enables them.**
* * *
For a century, the boldest exploiters in American capitalism have wanted exactly one thing: to know how desperate you are before they name a price.
What stopped them wasn't conscience. It was math. You cannot put a Pinkerton agent behind every coal miner, reading his mail, checking his bank balance, deciding in real time exactly how little he'd take to go back underground. The company store could bleed a whole town dry through debt and scrip, but it charged everyone the same price on the shelf. Even the most predatory boss in 1920 was working with a blunt instrument.
He didn't have an algorithm. Now everyone does.
The Pinkertons still tell you something true about this moment, even if their actual job was spying on union halls rather than reading ledgers. They were predatory capital's answer to a labor movement it couldn't control by other means -- surveillance and intimidation, aimed at people who were organizing precisely because they knew, collectively, that the company store was designed to keep them in debt forever.
What nobody in that fight had, on either side, was the ability to individualize it. To know that this miner, specifically, was three weeks behind on rent and would take almost anything.
The exploitation was real. It just couldn't be personal. It had to work at the scale of a town, not the scale of a person.
That constraint is gone. And the people doing the exploiting know it.
## Two words for the same machine
Economists and regulators have started calling this "surveillance pricing" when it happens to you as a buyer, and "algorithmic wage discrimination" when it happens to you as a worker - such as an Uber driver, which we'll get into shortly. They are the same tool pointed in two directions.
The Federal Trade Commission's own study of surveillance pricing -- not a partisan think tank, the federal agency itself -- is proof this isn't a fringe theory. In January 2025, FTC staff released preliminary findings from their investigation into the data brokers and pricing intermediaries that retailers use, and the findings were stark: companies were proven to be tracking consumer behavior down to mouse movements and abandoned shopping carts, and at least one set of intermediaries had worked with more than 250 retail clients to build **individualized pricing profiles** , so their clients could charge their customers **the highest price they 'd pay** \- for the same item, in the same market.
Alongside that report, the agency opened a public comment period built around one explicit question: **had gig workers or employees had their pay set - and changed - this same way?**
We don't actually know what the public said in answer, because almost nobody got the chance to finish saying it.
The comment window opened January 17, 2025, just 4 days before Trump's inauguration, and was shut down within days by the agency's incoming leadership -- a three-month comment period got cut to less than a week, closed before the gig-worker question, or any other question in it, got a real public answer.
One commissioner republished the agency's own questions under her own name just to keep them on the record; another formally objected to the closure of public comment. Neither objection reopened it. No final report followed. No rule followed.
**The federal government asked exactly the right question, on the record, and then made sure it would never have to sit with the answer.**
## **Surveillance pricing - how much will you pay?**
Here's what an "individualized pricing profile" actually means, because that phrase is built to sound too abstract to get angry about.
It means Kroger -- one of the largest grocery chains in the country -- ripping paper price tags off the shelf and replacing them with digital screens that can change a price storewide in seconds. In 2019, Kroger piloted shelf displays built with Microsoft that used cameras to estimate a shopper's age and gender in real time. Kroger says that specific pilot ended, and that it isn't charging two people in the same aisle two different prices for the same can of soup today.
**But** senators investigating the rollout found the underlying system is fully built to do exactly that -- and Kroger has never promised, in writing, that it won't. The price on the shelf might not be lying to you this week. It's just built to lie to you the moment the company decides it's profitable, and nothing in federal law requires you to be told when that switch flips.
It means Delta Air Lines telling its own investors it's using AI to help set ticket prices based on a prediction of "the amount people are willing to pay" -- until three U.S. senators warned the practice could mean charging each traveler up to their own personal "pain point," and forced a public walk-back. Delta CEO Ed Bastian now says the airline won't personalize fares using individual data. Nothing in federal law requires that promise to survive next quarter's earnings call.
And before AI made any of this easy, a travel booking site called Orbitz got caught steering Mac users toward pricier hotel rooms than PC users looking at the exact same room. Other travel sites got caught charging people more than $500 apart for the same hotel room on the same night, based on nothing but which city they were browsing from.
That was the crude version, built by hand. What the FTC's 250-client dataset describes is that same idea, industrialized: a system built to find, for each person, the single highest price they'll pay without walking away -- and charge them exactly that, while the person next to them in line, or clicking the same link a minute later, pays less and neither one of them ever finds out.
That's what's happening to your wallet. Now let's talk about what's happening to your paycheck, because "algorithm" is a word people use to make something feel unaccountable, and I don't think it should get to hide behind that.
## I've done this work. I know what it feels like from inside the app.
I've driven for DoorDash, when I was a broke college student raising a child alone. I've worked a UPS holiday season as a package driver, the stretch of the year when the volume triples and the route optimization software decides, minute by minute, how much slack you have -- which is to say, none. And before either of those, I worked for the United States Postal Service, a union job with a fixed route, a fixed wage, and a human being you could actually talk to if something went wrong.
I've lived on both sides of the line this essay is about. USPS is the old model: imperfect, but legible. You knew your rate. You knew your route. Nobody was quietly A/B testing your paycheck while you drove.
DoorDash and UPS's peak-season routing are the new model: a dispatch system that knows exactly how many deliveries you can be pushed to take - and how low of a wage you'll accept per job - before you decline one, and adjusts around that number, not around what the work is actually worth.
You feel it as a driver. You feel the app deciding something about you that you're never allowed to see. That's not a metaphor I picked up from a research paper. That's a Tuesday.
## The clearest case study: Uber drivers
Uber gives us the clearest paper trail, because Uber changed its own model out loud. Before 2022, when a passenger paid a surge price, the driver got paid a surge wage -- the multiplier flowed through proportionally. That was the deal. That was fair. And that's what brought drivers out onto the roads during rush hours, inclement weather, bad traffic, etc. matching supply to demand.
Then Uber shifted to what it calls "upfront pricing," which sounds like a customer-service win and is actually the opposite: **rider fares and driver pay are now calculated by separate algorithms, with no fixed relationship between them.**
Columbia Business School research found this shift let Uber raise what riders pay while simultaneously cutting what drivers earn, pushing the company's own cut of each fare from roughly 32 percent to more than 42 percent. The National Employment Law Project found the real number can run even higher -- up to 70 percent on individual rides -- and that Uber quietly stopped disclosing its take rate to the public at all as of early 2025.
Here's the part that should stop us cold: the algorithm doesn't just take more. **It learns you.** Researchers studying Uber's transition found the earnings decline was largest for drivers who almost never turned down a ride -- the algorithm was inferring, from each driver's own acceptance history, the least amount that driver would tolerate, and adjusting the offer **down** to meet it.
It used to be if you paid a surge price, your driver got a surge wage. Now the two aren't even calculated by the same equation.
None of this is a matter of interpretation, because the person running the company has admitted it himself. Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi has publicly acknowledged that the company adjusts driver pay based on individual behavioral patterns -- after years of Uber flatly denying that exact accusation when drivers and researchers made it. He kept his job. His personal wealth, built mostly from Uber stock, is estimated in the hundreds of millions of dollars.
The person profiting most from this practice is not confused about how it works.
## The desperation tax
If Uber drivers are the visible case, here's the one that should genuinely alarm you: it's already come for nurses. And some of the same money is behind it.
DoorDash's co-founder and CEO, Tony Xu -- the same DoorDash whose app I drove -- is a personal investor in Clipboard Health, one of the largest "gig nursing" platforms in the country. Xu became a billionaire the day DoorDash went public in 2020.
This isn't three separate industries independently landing on the same bad idea. **It 's the same investor class running the same playbook against whichever workforce hasn't organized against it yet.**
Clipboard Health, co-run by Wei Deng and Bo Lu, is one of four major platforms now applying this model to nursing -- alongside ShiftKey (CEO Mike Vitek), IntelyCare (CEO and co-founder David Coppins), and Nursa (founder and CEO Curtis Anderson). Each of these companies is now valued somewhere between roughly $1 billion and $2 billion.
**Reporting on these platforms has found they buy data-broker profiles on individual nurses, including signals about their credit card debt and broader financial distress, and use that information to lowball shift offers to the workers who can least afford to say no.** Same license. Same shift. Same patients. Same work. Different pay, priced not to the work itself but to how badly you need the money.
I want to give that practice a name simpler than "algorithmic wage discrimination," because most people are never going to say that phrase out loud, and they shouldn't have to in order to understand they're being robbed by it. Call it what it is: **a desperation tax.**
It's a tax collected not by the government, but by a private algorithm, assessed not on your income, but on your need -- and it goes straight into a corporation's profit margin and a megamillionaire's pocket, not into a single road, school, or hospital that serves you back.
## How Uber became the whole life cycle of the problem
It's worth sitting with the fact that Uber isn't just one example among many -- it's the entire arc, start to finish. Under founding CEO Travis Kalanick, it undercut the taxi industry on price until most of the competition was gone.
In doing that, it helped gut a decade of public transit investment: researchers at the University of Kentucky found that when Uber and Lyft enter a city, rail ridership falls roughly 1.3 percent a year and bus ridership roughly 1.7 percent, cumulatively -- enough that San Francisco's bus ridership dropped nearly 13 percent since Uber arrived there, and enough that transit systems would need to expand service by a quarter just to hold ridership flat against the trend.
That's real money, real routes, and real years that could have gone into public buses and trains, spent instead subsidizing a company that was still losing money for most of a decade in order to take over the market.
And having taken it over -- having become, in huge swaths of the country, the only game in town -- Uber turned the same surveillance apparatus it built to win riders against the drivers who now have nowhere else to go.
This is the pattern researchers and writers covering platform economics have started calling "enshittification": a company locks in users and workers first, then squeezes them once they can't easily leave.
It's not a conspiracy theory. Economist Lindsay Owens's forthcoming book on corporate pricing schemes, "**Gouged "**, treats this as a documented, spreading category of corporate behavior -- not an edge case, a business model.
## Congress has failed here, specifically, not vaguely
Four concrete failures, not a general complaint:
**First** , the FTC's own study -- the one that opened this essay -- got shelved by the same agency that ran it, before the public it asked for comment could even finish answering. That's not a failure of research. It's a failure of leadership, integrity, and durability: nothing forces an agency's findings to survive a change in leadership unless Congress writes that into law. Congress hasn't.
**Second** , a real bill exists and is going nowhere. Representative Greg Casar's **Stop AI Price Gouging and Wage Fixing Act** would directly restrict the use of algorithmic systems to set individualized prices and wages -- the exact practice this essay describes. It has sat languishing in committee while the practice it targets keeps spreading.
**Third** , the states are doing Congress's job for it. Two dozen states have introduced more than forty bills to rein in surveillance pricing since the start of 2026 -- including right here in Washington, where HB 2481 was introduced this year to prohibit surveillance-based price discrimination. Maryland has already signed a ban into law. Connecticut followed. That is what it looks like when state legislators move faster than the federal government whose actual job this is.
**Fourth** , and most recently: in March 2026, the House Oversight Committee opened its own investigation into surveillance pricing, sending letters to major travel and platform companies demanding documentation on their pricing algorithms. An investigation is not a law. A letter is not a subpoena. But it is, at minimum, an admission from Congress itself that the problem is real and Americans are suffering -- more than a year after the FTC already informed them it was, and then got told to stop asking.
## What Congress could do -- three fixes, straight up
1\. Ban the use of financial-distress data specifically to individualize wages or shift offers -- not just prices, **wages**. A worker's medical debt is not a legitimate input into what they get paid for the same job.
2\. Require real disclosure. If an algorithm is setting your pay or your price, you should be able to see what data went into that number, the same way you can ask to see your own credit report.
3\. Give the FTC's own findings teeth. Turn what's left of the 6(b) study -- the preliminary findings that survived, the public comment period that didn't -- into a mandated rulemaking with an actual deadline, so a change in the White House can't simply switch it off next time.
## Where this leaves us
The tool changed. The appetite didn't. What the coal bosses wanted, Uber's investors got: a way to know exactly how little a person will accept, and to charge them -- or pay them -- accordingly, one desperate person at a time.
The only real question left is whether the people we send to Congress understand that the fight for a fair wage and the fight for a fair price are now, literally, running on the same algorithm.
I've driven the routes. I've seen the app decide. I'm running because I don't think that fight should be left to a handful of state legislatures while Washington, D.C. looks the other way.
**Care. Courage. The Constitution.**

Let's get into it. | | ---|---|--- | | | Forwarded this email? ? for more ? Wage suppression on one side. Price increase on the other. Basic foundations of commerce in society - equal pay for equal work, the same price for all - are no longer holding. Let's get into it. | | | Aug 3 | | | | | | | | | | | | Fair businesses strengthen countries, helping the economy and everyone in it. Unfair, highly exploitative, and predatory mega-businesses degrade and destroy the nation that enables them. For a century, the boldest exploiters in American capitalism have wanted exactly one thing: to know how desperate you are before they name a price. What stopped them wasn't conscience. It was math. You cannot put a Pinkerton agent behind every coal miner, reading his mail, checking his bank balance, deciding in real time exactly how little he'd take to go back underground. The company store could bleed a whole town dry through debt and scrip, but it charged everyone the same price on the shelf. Even the most predatory boss in 1920 was working with a blunt instrument. He didn't have an algorithm. Now everyone does. The Pinkertons still tell you something true about this moment, even if their actual job was spying on union halls rather than reading ledgers. They were predatory capital's answer to a labor movement it couldn't control by other means -- surveillance and intimidation, aimed at people who were organizing precisely because they knew, collectively, that the company store was designed to keep them in debt forever. What nobody in that fight had, on either side, was the ability to individualize it. To know that this miner, specifically, was three weeks behind on rent and would take almost anything. The exploitation was real. It just couldn't be personal. It had to work at the scale of a town, not the scale of a person. That constraint is gone. And the people doing the exploiting know it. Two words for the same machine Economists and regulators have started calling this "surveillance pricing" when it happens to you as a buyer, and "algorithmic wage discrimination" when it happens to you as a worker - such as an Uber driver, which we'll get into shortly. They are the same tool pointed in two directions. The Federal Trade Commission's own study of surveillance pricing -- not a partisan think tank, the federal agency itself -- is proof this isn't a fringe theory. In January 2025, FTC staff released preliminary findings from their investigation into the data brokers and pricing intermediaries that retailers use, and the findings were stark: companies were proven to be tracking consumer behavior down to mouse movements and abandoned shopping carts, and at least one set of intermediaries had worked with more than 250 retail clients to build individualized pricing profiles , so their clients could charge their customers the highest price they 'd pay \- for the same item, in the same market. Alongside that report, the agency opened a public comment period built around one explicit question: had gig workers or employees had their pay set - and changed - this same way? We don't actually know what the public said in answer, because almost nobody got the chance to finish saying it. The comment window opened January 17, 2025, just 4 days before Trump's inauguration, and was shut down within days by the agency's incoming leadership -- a three-month comment period got cut to less than a week, closed before the gig-worker question, or any other question in it, got a real public answer. One commissioner republished the agency's own questions under her own name just to keep them on the record; another formally objected to the closure of public comment. Neither objection reopened it. No final report followed. No rule followed. The federal government asked exactly the right question, on the record, and then made sure it would never have to sit with the answer. Surveillance pricing - how much will you pay? Here's what an "individualized pricing profile" actually means, because that phrase is built to sound too abstract to get angry about. It means Kroger -- one of the largest grocery chains in the country -- ripping paper price tags off the shelf and replacing them with digital screens that can change a price storewide in seconds. In 2019, Kroger piloted shelf displays built with Microsoft that used cameras to estimate a shopper's age and gender in real time. Kroger says that specific pilot ended, and that it isn't charging two people in the same aisle two different prices for the same can of soup today. But senators investigating the rollout found the underlying system is fully built to do exactly that -- and Kroger has never promised, in writing, that it won't. The price on the shelf might not be lying to you this week. It's just built to lie to you the moment the company decides it's profitable, and nothing in federal law requires you to be told when that switch flips. It means Delta Air Lines telling its own investors it's using AI to help set ticket prices based on a prediction of "the amount people are willing to pay" -- until three U.S. senators warned the practice could mean charging each traveler up to their own personal "pain point," and forced a public walk-back. Delta CEO Ed Bastian now says the airline won't personalize fares using individual data. Nothing in federal law requires that promise to survive next quarter's earnings call. And before AI made any of this easy, a travel booking site called Orbitz got caught steering Mac users toward pricier hotel rooms than PC users looking at the exact same room. Other travel sites got caught charging people more than $500 apart for the same hotel room on the same night, based on nothing but which city they were browsing from. That was the crude version, built by hand. What the FTC's 250-client dataset describes is that same idea, industrialized: a system built to find, for each person, the single highest price they'll pay without walking away -- and charge them exactly that, while the person next to them in line, or clicking the same link a minute later, pays less and neither one of them ever finds out. That's what's happening to your wallet. Now let's talk about what's happening to your paycheck, because "algorithm" is a word people use to make something feel unaccountable, and I don't think it should get to hide behind that. I've done this work. I know what it feels like from inside the app. I've driven for DoorDash, when I was a broke college student raising a child alone. I've worked a UPS holiday season as a package driver, the stretch of the year when the volume triples and the route optimization software decides, minute by minute, how much slack you have -- which is to say, none. And before either of those, I worked for the United States Postal Service, a union job with a fixed route, a fixed wage, and a human being you could actually talk to if something went wrong. I've lived on both sides of the line this essay is about. USPS is the old model: imperfect, but legible. You knew your rate. You knew your route. Nobody was quietly A/B testing your paycheck while you drove. DoorDash and UPS's peak-season routing are the new model: a dispatch system that knows exactly how many deliveries you can be pushed to take - and how low of a wage you'll accept per job - before you decline one, and adjusts around that number, not around what the work is actually worth. You feel it as a driver. You feel the app deciding something about you that you're never allowed to see. That's not a metaphor I picked up from a research paper. That's a Tuesday. The clearest case study: Uber drivers Uber gives us the clearest paper trail, because Uber changed its own model out loud. Before 2022, when a passenger paid a surge price, the driver got paid a surge wage -- the multiplier flowed through proportionally. That was the deal. That was fair. And that's what brought drivers out onto the roads during rush hours, inclement weather, bad traffic, etc. matching supply to demand. Then Uber shifted to what it calls "upfront pricing," which sounds like a customer-service win and is actually the opposite: rider fares and driver pay are now calculated by separate algorithms, with no fixed relationship between them. Columbia Business School research found this shift let Uber raise what riders pay while simultaneously cutting what drivers earn, pushing the company's own cut of each fare from roughly 32 percent to more than 42 percent. The National Employment Law Project found the real number can run even higher -- up to 70 percent on individual rides -- and that Uber quietly stopped disclosing its take rate to the public at all as of early 2025. Here's the part that should stop us cold: the algorithm doesn't just take more. It learns you. Researchers studying Uber's transition found the earnings decline was largest for drivers who almost never turned down a ride -- the algorithm was inferring, from each driver's own acceptance history, the least amount that driver would tolerate, and adjusting the offer down to meet it. It used to be if you paid a surge price, your driver got a surge wage. Now the two aren't even calculated by the same equation. None of this is a matter of interpretation, because the person running the company has admitted it himself. Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi has publicly acknowledged that the company adjusts driver pay based on individual behavioral patterns -- after years of Uber flatly denying that exact accusation when drivers and researchers made it. He kept his job. His personal wealth, built mostly from Uber stock, is estimated in the hundreds of millions of dollars. The person profiting most from this practice is not confused about how it works. The desperation tax If Uber drivers are the visible case, here's the one that should genuinely alarm you: it's already come for nurses. And some of the same money is behind it. DoorDash's co-founder and CEO, Tony Xu -- the same DoorDash whose app I drove -- is a personal investor in Clipboard Health, one of the largest "gig nursing" platforms in the country. Xu became a billionaire the day DoorDash went public in 2020. This isn't three separate industries independently landing on the same bad idea. It 's the same investor class running the same playbook against whichever workforce hasn't organized against it yet. Clipboard Health, co-run by Wei Deng and Bo Lu, is one of four major platforms now applying this model to nursing -- alongside ShiftKey (CEO Mike Vitek), IntelyCare (CEO and co-founder David Coppins), and Nursa (founder and CEO Curtis Anderson). Each of these companies is now valued somewhere between roughly $1 billion and $2 billion. Reporting on these platforms has found they buy data-broker profiles on individual nurses, including signals about their credit card debt and broader financial distress, and use that information to lowball shift offers to the workers who can least afford to say no. Same license. Same shift. Same patients. Same work. Different pay, priced not to the work itself but to how badly you need the money. I want to give that practice a name simpler than "algorithmic wage discrimination," because most people are never going to say that phrase out loud, and they shouldn't have to in order to understand they're being robbed by it. Call it what it is: a desperation tax. It's a tax collected not by the government, but by a private algorithm, assessed not on your income, but on your need -- and it goes straight into a corporation's profit margin and a megamillionaire's pocket, not into a single road, school, or hospital that serves you back. How Uber became the whole life cycle of the problem It's worth sitting with the fact that Uber isn't just one example among many -- it's the entire arc, start to finish. Under founding CEO Travis Kalanick, it undercut the taxi industry on price until most of the competition was gone. In doing that, it helped gut a decade of public transit investment: researchers at the University of Kentucky found that when Uber and Lyft enter a city, rail ridership falls roughly 1.3 percent a year and bus ridership roughly 1.7 percent, cumulatively -- enough that San Francisco's bus ridership dropped nearly 13 percent since Uber arrived there, and enough that transit systems would need to expand service by a quarter just to hold ridership flat against the trend. That's real money, real routes, and real years that could have gone into public buses and trains, spent instead subsidizing a company that was still losing money for most of a decade in order to take over the market. And having taken it over -- having become, in huge swaths of the country, the only game in town -- Uber turned the same surveillance apparatus it built to win riders against the drivers who now have nowhere else to go. This is the pattern researchers and writers covering platform economics have started calling "enshittification": a company locks in users and workers first, then squeezes them once they can't easily leave. It's not a conspiracy theory. Economist Lindsay Owens's forthcoming book on corporate pricing schemes, "Gouged ", treats this as a documented, spreading category of corporate behavior -- not an edge case, a business model. Congress has failed here, specifically, not vaguely Four concrete failures, not a general complaint: First , the FTC's own study -- the one that opened this essay -- got shelved by the same agency that ran it, before the public it asked for comment could even finish answering. That's not a failure of research. It's a failure of leadership, integrity, and durability: nothing forces an agency's findings to survive a change in leadership unless Congress writes that into law. Congress hasn't. Second , a real bill exists and is going nowhere. Representative Greg Casar's Stop AI Price Gouging and Wage Fixing Act would directly restrict the use of algorithmic systems to set individualized prices and wages -- the exact practice this essay describes. It has sat languishing in committee while the practice it targets keeps spreading. Third , the states are doing Congress's job for it. Two dozen states have introduced more than forty bills to rein in surveillance pricing since the start of 2026 -- including right here in Washington, where HB 2481 was introduced this year to prohibit surveillance-based price discrimination. Maryland has already signed a ban into law. Connecticut followed. That is what it looks like when state legislators move faster than the federal government whose actual job this is. Fourth , and most recently: in March 2026, the House Oversight Committee opened its own investigation into surveillance pricing, sending letters to major travel and platform companies demanding documentation on their pricing algorithms. An investigation is not a law. A letter is not a subpoena. But it is, at minimum, an admission from Congress itself that the problem is real and Americans are suffering -- more than a year after the FTC already informed them it was, and then got told to stop asking. What Congress could do -- three fixes, straight up 1\. Ban the use of financial-distress data specifically to individualize wages or shift offers -- not just prices, wages. A worker's medical debt is not a legitimate input into what they get paid for the same job. 2\. Require real disclosure. If an algorithm is setting your pay or your price, you should be able to see what data went into that number, the same way you can ask to see your own credit report. 3\. Give the FTC's own findings teeth. Turn what's left of the 6(b) study -- the preliminary findings that survived, the public comment period that didn't -- into a mandated rulemaking with an actual deadline, so a change in the White House can't simply switch it off next time. Where this leaves us The tool changed. The appetite didn't. What the coal bosses wanted, Uber's investors got: a way to know exactly how little a person will accept, and to charge them -- or pay them -- accordingly, one desperate person at a time. The only real question left is whether the people we send to Congress understand that the fight for a fair wage and the fight for a fair price are now, literally, running on the same algorithm. I've driven the routes. I've seen the app decide. I'm running because I don't think that fight should be left to a handful of state legislatures while Washington, D.C. looks the other way. Care. Courage. The Constitution.** | | ---|---|--- You 're currently a free subscriber to "It's a Matter of Integrity" by Melissa Chaudhry. body:
Please read for details of how to obtain a replacement ballot if needed.

| | | | | | | All,Each day as we all learn more about the devastation of the fires in Spokane, I will try to keep you updated.We have cancelled the election night gathering we had scheduled tomorrow at The Swinging Doors in north Spokane. The restaurant has been in the evacuation zone and they are currently closed.
Earlier today I visited the temporary evacuation shelter at the Spokane Convention Center and talked to dozens of people who are displaced or have lost their homes. Many are elderly and do not have family or friends nearby. Teams of volunteers are doing an amazing job providing critical support and care around the clock.
Yesterday, I met with local leaders in a strong bipartisan response. I talked to the White House and head of the Department of Homeland Security to ensure that they are well aware of our challenges and are working to secure federal assistance.
For those who want to vote in the primary election tomorrow and do not have access to their ballot, a replacement ballot can be picked up at the Spokane County Elections Office, 1033 W. Gardner Avenue (open tomorrow 7am to 8pm), or the voter service center at CenterPlace, 2426 N. Discovery Place, Spokane Valley (7am to 8pm). If you have access to a printer (or can visit a local library to access one) you can print a replacement ballot by visiting voteWA.gov.
Eleanor and I are remembering the families who are displaced and have lost their homes, and deeply appreciate the first responders, firefighters, National Guard members, pilots and law enforcement officers and volunteers who are still working overtime to protect life and property and to care for those in need.
The important thing now is to put politics aside and focus on the important work of governing, ensuring a coordinated response among City, County, State and federal officials.
I hope in the future when people look back on this tragedy, they will be able to say that elected officials and civil servants from both parties, from all levels of government, worked together to put the fires out and help those in need.
-Michael

_It’s pure evil, team._

body:
Protect the Vote & Secure Wisconsin Elections
No images? [Click here](https://republicanpartyofwisconsin.cmail19.com/t/y-e-fyukljd-didthutlhu-n/) [](https://republicanpartyofwisconsin.cmail19.com/t/y-l-fyukljd-didthutlhu-r/) Patriot,**_Election Integrity Update_** The **August Primary is only 8 days away** , and Wisconsin needs volunteers ready to Protect the Vote.The Primary is our first test before the high-stakes **November General Election**. Every trained election observer and poll worker helps ensure election laws are followed, increases transparency, and strengthens confidence in Wisconsin's elections.As President Trump recently emphasized, the stakes this November couldn't be higher. Wisconsin will once again be at the center of the national election, and protecting every legal vote starts with volunteers willing to serve.If you're interested in becoming an election observer or are already a Republican-nominated poll worker, **create or access your volunteer account today** using the link below and join the Wisconsin Protect the Vote team.**Step up. Get trained. Protect the Vote.** [Sign Up For A Volunteer Account](https://republicanpartyofwisconsin.cmail19.com/t/y-l-fyukljd-didthutlhu-y/) **_Upcoming Training Sessions_ - Election Observers or Workers**Election observers and workers fill vital roles in ensuring election integrity. They receive the training they need to identify Election Day irregularities and support our rapid-response team of legal professionals.Election observers and workers primarily oversee **early vote and election day processes.** All observers participating in the Protect the Vote election observer program are _required to attend one training session._ Below are training sessions offered statewide. The statewide schedule of training sessions for election observers or poll workers can be found below:**8/4: Zoom, 6:00pm-7:30pm**. If you are interested in this session, you can [**_RSVP here._**](https://republicanpartyofwisconsin.cmail19.com/t/y-l-fyukljd-didthutlhu-j/)**8/5: Zoom, 12:00pm-1:30pm**. If you are interested in this session, you can [**_RSVP here._**](https://republicanpartyofwisconsin.cmail19.com/t/y-l-fyukljd-didthutlhu-t/)**8/8: Zoom, 10:00am-11:00am**. If you are interested in this session, you can [**_RSVP here._**](https://republicanpartyofwisconsin.cmail19.com/t/y-l-fyukljd-didthutlhu-i/)**_Upcoming Training Sessions_ - ****Special Monitors** Special monitors serve similar goals as election observers/workers, but across a broader range of situations. They receive the training they need to oversee machine testing, view absentee ballot processing, and post-election canvasses.Special monitors primarily observe **pre- and post-election processes.** Like election observers, all volunteers participating in the Protect the Vote special monitor program are _required to attend one training session._ The statewide schedule for training sessions for special monitors can be found below:**8/6: 6:00pm-7:30pm.** If you are interested in this session, you can **[_RSVP here._](https://republicanpartyofwisconsin.cmail19.com/t/y-l-fyukljd-didthutlhu-d/)*****ALL TRAINING IS OPEN TO ANYONE INTERESTED, INCLUDING POLL WORKERS. **Good Morning!** On this day in 1790, Congress authorized a fleet of [10 boats](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLGunDAQAL_GdEb24ge-wkUaukubEu3hBfZk7JNtQOTro0TKF7x6pNFofj2nJ3LguP7EnVxd0hTpKoFqpTzdFDOV-aA1Yd0IPfmcXqniBAp6qaxUZvLI4Z5M491CBNQ15PRgv2xnTW-bzSGSQWNo6EGTMsNsXmqx_jXP1lirTMPur01ZZbTSBvoWOloeAA_d9Ur32gqjyHNNuX0njnWjJdzppNzOaW-C22r9FNH9EDAKGK_rao8SuU15FTDuuOJvjlQEjBFPDHLjUlO-5X8iYASlvwSMeKxHqQLGhS6JeScvTyqFQpHvw_PM6SjhlqVi5RTJN9n5z8UhcOkHYdS6I4d_UfVbJ08HfwIAAP__lMKJlQ) to chase down smugglers and collect tariffs along the coast. That little squadron, the Revenue Cutter Service, eventually became the U.S. Coast Guard, which turns 236 today. Even the biggest decisions get made by people with to-do lists. Washington and Tokyo confirmed yesterday that they teamed up to prop up the sagging yen, their first joint currency intervention in 15 years. The tell came days earlier, when photographers at a Camp David cabinet meeting zoomed in on Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's [notepad and found one line](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0LGupiAQBeCnwQ4DI1exoNjG7m67pZlfh19uEAyMv_HtN-4rbHOak3w5OX--528MMaT3b9zJsc9zoqtGYqYy35QK1eWkd0beCFdaS35lxhkU9FJZqcy8Yoj3bJrVeSKgriGnB_tlO2t622xuoFFhj6MFWNB6tPBlvbE4QPfyozZNcI-mrDJaaQN9Cx35EWDUXa90r60witbAubQ_OSTeyMc7f6i0S96b6Dbmo4rul4BJwHRdV7uk1_KUAqaHFjAp-4QWMJ1VciGsZ7llSEzlQ4mq5CzreRy5sLwpSfRMRf7ggUlWpqPKkKTnduM9NsWtxxViDLUfhFHvHUP8t4X_68CPg78BAAD__z3chDg): "Buy Japanese Yen (JPY) $5-10 bil." We have details below. What if the biggest threat in your diet isn't sugar or fat, but something hiding in more than half of everything you eat? Ultra-processed foods have been linked to plenty of chronic conditions, all of which can shorten your life. And they're lurking in products you'd never suspect, from your morning bagel to the sauce on your stir-fry. The good news? You don't have to overhaul your kitchen or your budget to cut them out. On today's episode of _The Flyover Podcast_ , Ayla reveals six everyday swaps that push these foods off your plate, plus the one trick that exposes them on any label. [Tune in here!](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykzzFuwyAUgOHTwBYLHpjggaFLtnTtiF7Ms02FjYVfk_r2VXuFHuD_pe_jHu-YS97md1wp8FTjRq-jEDO1eNLW6Bi_aK7IC2Gi1OqjMkZQ4C7KX5SNCXM5o5UpTERARlLQV997463zcgm6H8w1JdVPFjW6ZB9oDAy96f04Ggsyh9-b8spqpS24DgxNA8CgjVPaaS-sopS5tu6z5o0XmspZn9S6sa6yhIV5P4R5E3ATcGv0aLilrpwCbntN9M0NtWwh7a9cSj7cVVg1r5jLX8__Qj8D_AQAAP__aqpp4g) You can't predict when an emergency will happen, but you can be prepared for one. ## Blanche Scraps Fund to Save AG Nomination
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche rescinded a $1.8 billion ["anti-weaponization" fund](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLGu4yAQRb_G7ohgIIQUFNu4e9tuaY1hbLMiYMG8WPn7lfcXXnelK13dc_58zV-Ycirbb3yR57XOhc6eiZna_KHSqIdv2iryThgptrpUxhkkWCGdkGaOmPJnNmP0KxGQHsmrh7s77Yx14-5hMfbpgrZh0aTxoa0JQGi1lOahNIzJX2vSSaOkMmBvoGl9AjyVtlJZ5QYjKSau7fa3psI7rflT39Ruob7G7Hfmow_61wDTANN5nreyhIvi6geYjpoTp9AHmEItW6N-RQycyiZwE1xjFEvGEnYSjTDs1EUkzGKvOdZvFp0Kcm1dUIlCuUVg4SROwkO0UPD-lHe4j83H40w5p24fg5HbC1P-f5F_5PXt4V8AAAD__zSrjQQ) Sunday, striking a deal with Republican holdouts that revived his stalled nomination to lead the Justice Department. The fund came from President Trump's settlement with the IRS over the leak of his tax returns and would have paid people claiming they were victims of [government weaponization](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLGOhCAYhJ8GOwwCh1hQXGO3115pEH6VC_Jv8L81vv3FfYXrJpnMTOb7fkwPn3Iq65ffwdGCU4HzyEAEdbqgVDjCL6zoaQMfIVackfwkhTRcWC70FH3K16Sb6BYACaoB1_X2wyqrjW02N5jYRxGU1ssSwyxMP_RxCMqqQUcjRJPc3Sas0J3otDStVLAMUg6dMqIznWVaQEyEtf3BVGiDJV_4gtoG3JvsNqLnwdQnkyOT43mebZiP-8XtMznekskxYC1X4ZRyTgcnjJHP2ZewAfdEWAtcfIUC1WdecE_FU8LC5NhUF5_nO2Z6psW6-5Tf2_QvYC8n_wIAAP__r0SAzw). Lawmakers in both parties worried Jan. 6 convicts could cash in. Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, who had threatened to [block the confirmation](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkL2SpCAURp9GMyz-GjEg2MSsN93QQrwo2ygUXNvx7ad6XmHir-qrc86_5_S0IYZj_Wt3MOjTdMBVIyBCmW44ClR3wposbmAXWEqaE9qJU64I1YTKabEh3pNsF-MBOIgWDOv1QwstlW43o3vtZqqcl8JSkMNDO6H64UGFptRp1gbzeaOaSkaZ5KrjAvzA-cCEokwx3UgKS8BUuv8pHLiBj3d6Q-lc2ttoNsRcG_Gn4WPDx-u6Op--PhafveFjTjFgcLXhI5Zzz5XYleTgXiR5T2LwQOqZcypIrEco5AU3KZDPOQZnD1JghlhJgQgHtsUs-Qoxhqr6RtJ1tyH-gOCv6r0N_w4AAP__7SuFcw), announced their support Monday after the department also limited the settlement's tax audit immunity to Trump, his sons, and the Trump Organization. The Senate Judiciary Committee is now [expected to advance](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0LGOtCAUBeCnwU6DF0SmoPgbu_nbLc0FrsoEYYLsGN9-477CNqc5yXeS8_WcnxhiSOt_3MnUJc-JziNSrVTmi1Khw33TmrFuhJ58yTZXnIGDarluuZw9hnjNsvFmIQISDZl-1IMWWirdbEbgKMjZRQhEa5X2bnADqtH2MIxWDU0wt8Y1lz3vJagOBC0PgEcvFO9Vr5nk5EPNpXvlkOpGS7zyh0rn8t5Es9X6Ppj4x2BiMJ3n2blk3V0ymG6awcT1HYLBVLP3rY2Y3Eatz68W1_aghJVal0u6UrfVPTbF-PcZYgyHGpnk644h_u7VP530MfATAAD__35peaQ) the nomination when it meets this morning.
## Iran Denies Talks After Trump Halts Strikes
President Trump announced that [new talks with Iran](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLFyhCAYhJ9GOxwEVCwo0thd2pTOL_yc5BBu8Pecy9NnzCuk3N2Znd3v6zbfIMSQ7p-woSGf54TnHpEIy_zGVHC3B94z0Irg0JW8ZIJZcNEzrhlXs4MQ37OqnfGIAmWNph10p6VWva5XM7plEIMfvJai071aRte1DsFKHL22Qx3M1cY1Vy1vlegbIdGPQoyt7Hnbt7pSHF2gXJrvHBKt6OM7v7A0Nm91NCvRc6_kRyWmSkzneTZpsdeLK7-cXKKrxBQKpEpMVI7tyS7BCOJjZ0AE9rEzC8liRMfWXLbjh6XDRoTCik3QjbyTXV2Me54hxrD3Q6X4fYMQ_1bQv9C9jPgNAAD__8Dzg9E) would begin yesterday afternoon after he called off a planned attack he said would have been the biggest since World War II. Tehran quickly denied that. Iran's foreign ministry said yesterday there were [no direct negotiations](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0LFuhSAYBeCnwQ2DPxRxYOjidrt2NCi_SoNg4L_X3Ldv7Ct0OctJvpOc78f0cCGGtH25Ay2teUp41YhEWKY3poJ1eeKWHe3oPPqS50xuAgGaC8OFmrwL8T2pxtsVEVA2aLvefBhplDbNbs1qhJ_7Wc5SG4WLH1a_OnQKtB76YWiCvTVhhOpEp0C3IHEdAIZOatHpzjAl0AfKpf3JIdGOa3znF5Z2yUcT7U50ViY_GYwMxuu62iXNy10yGG-awSjMHZLBSOV5nDwUl_iz8oRbpuAo5FT5iW5BfpZ85upi5e1OR2yK9ecVYgxV90yJ7XAh_i3Tv-56WfgNAAD__6CiffE) planned with Washington, only discussions with neighboring Oman about the shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz. Trump fired back on Truth Social, branding Iran's leadership "unbelievably duplicitous," though he said he scrapped the attack partly at the urging of Gulf allies, including Saudi Arabia. [See the post here](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0LFuwyAQxvGngS3RcVBMBoZKlbd0qtTRwuYcU2FjwSVR3r5yX6Hr90m_4f99Ha4h5bTdPsNKnucybPRsmZipDi_aKrXpTrcSeKEQKdYyFg4DAtoTuBOYIYaUX4OR0c9ESFqSV517c9oZ6-TiR6Oim2C8UADQgGGkiNhNTuFklCKZ_KGBA6NAGbRn1DRfEC9KW1BWOWGAYuJSzz8lbbzQnF_lQfU8lVVmvzDvTeh3gb3Anuudl1amFPLxH6OBSiF_lC3k-FXv6y6w30vjJrBXqgON2CGiQ-PAWVl93J8p59RsJwzc1pD-KMn_6vPw-BsAAP__vqJ2mQ). Back in Washington, lawmakers from both parties have voiced frustration with the administration over a lack of information on the conflict, now in its sixth month. [Follow live updates here](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLGOtCAURp8GOwwgP2JB8Td2s-2WBuWqdxfBwHXMvP1m9hW2_pIv55zPx_TwGDFtH_4AR2ueEtw1AhGU6QWpQF0u2LKnHXyAUPKcyU9KKMOF5UJPwWN8TboJbgVQ0DXgZG__2c5qY5vdyaH3WpreLrOBeRlm08MsNAxDLzrhTYPu_Sas0FJIrUyrOlgHpQbZGSGNtEwLCEi5tF8ZE-2wxld-QmmXfDTR7URnZd1_pkamxvu-22Wub4v3ztQY8Qn8OoMnqEyNWHzity885ORj4FSu4-RX5QESQuUJtkzoCXOqfIYNE69U8BsqX3yMEHheV6bGprhw3hgjVtMzLbbDY_xFoj91fDr1EwAA__-fv4kc).
## US, Japan Team Up to Prop Up Sliding Yen
The United States and Japan carried out their [first joint currency intervention](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0LGOszAQBOCnMR1oWRvHKVz8DV3-9kpk8BIcOXZkb8Lx9ifuFa6ZZqRvpPm6TTcXYkj3_-5Jltc8JdprJGYq00GpUF3edM-ON3KefMlzZjchoG7BtKAm70I8JtV4uxIhyYZsfzGDkUZp02xWDxpXWGEBMEhw8YOZB1TXZdaDlAs1wZ4aGFA99Ap1h5LWK-K1lxp63RuhgHzgXLpHDok3WuORP1S6JT-baDfmVxXyn8BR4Ljve-e-Q65nK3A8bYEjmDOkwPGg1D7cy6WWC7n6Lkc7U62UuCnWv_YQY6j6IhTcny7E3xH-0zMfiz8BAAD__6pVdT0) since 2011 on Friday, buying yen in a bid to halt the Japanese currency's slide. The dollar touched a [40-year high](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLGOwyAQRL_G7mzBmhAoKK5xl2uvtDawjslhsPAmkf_-lPzCdTPSaGb0fi7TBWOK-faNKzmey5TptSdipjodlCvt_kG3grwQBgq1XAvjBAJ0J0wn1BQwpmNSbXAzEdDQkpNnczKDUdq0i5uD9adgpTbiKtSZ_IBXK1BS0F5psm107zZhhJJCKtA9DDRbACsHLaSWplGCQuRS-3uJmRea01GeVHtf1ja5hXnbm-GrgbGBcY4Zs6f-wKWUd6KBccX6S7w3MPpHrZR9pLfBytGnj3zs3R03zN1nIR1dzEz1SZm6rZatEyBgsOZk-oXX1FYXtldMKe763ChxWzGmzxv-F8Kng78AAAD__82shjM) of 164 yen last month, driving up the cost of food, fuel, and other imports for Japanese households. The effort was not exactly a secret. A photographer at a Camp David cabinet meeting caught Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's notepad, which read, "To Do: Buy Japanese Yen (JPY) $5-10 bil." [See the photo here](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJyk0LGupiAQBeCnwQ4DI1exoNjG7m67pZlfh19uEAyMv_HtN-4rbHOak3w5OX--528MMaT3b9zJsc9zoqtGYqYy35QK1eWkd0beCFdaS35lxhkU9FJZqcy8Yoj3bJrVeSKgriGnB_tlO2t622xuoFFhj6MFWNB6tPBlvbE4QPfyozZNcI-mrDJaaQN9Cx35EWDUXa90r60witbAubQ_OSTeyMc7f6i0S96b6Dbmo4rul4BJwHRdV7uk1_KUAqaHFjAp-4QWMJ1VciGsZ7llSEzlQ4mq5CzreRy5sLwpSfRMRf7ggUlWpqPKkKTnduM9NsWtxxViDLUfhFHvHUP8t4X_68CPg78BAAD__z3chDg). The deal helped America, too. Japan [borrowed dollars](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkLHS2yAQhJ8GdXjghGVcUKRR96dNqUFiJZNg8MBZ_-jtM3KRF0h3c7Ozu9_--pq-fEwxbz_9E47XMmV8twRm1OlArmjLG1vx_IAPCLXMhf1EigaprFRmCj6mYzJdcCtA6Ds4fbNX21sz2O7hrDekh5vydh18ID_rvl9wn8N1uerlbrroTjdlldFKGxou1GO9E911Pyg9aCuMQohc6uV3iZkfWNNRdtTLUp5dcg_mVxP9D0GjoPFZMo7Lu50Yp0DQGPOOxjFvgsbzLWj0leOScJ7_UEjQOKM1ZJYVPhySi6x4wbP8BMsDWcbMqDsyx5Llu25oco7bhipXBDn75U_j8uqqC6_vmFJsw00YtT19TJ--_F8j747-BgAA___xKJJ9) against its U.S. Treasury holdings instead of selling them, sparing bond markets and keeping a lid on American borrowing costs, and Bessent said both allies stand ready to intervene again.
