# Turn Out on Tuesday
---
| | | | | | | | | | | |

[](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/rob-tracinski-1)

If you haven’t already voted early in the Fifth District Democratic primary, remember to turn out today for in-person voting at your local polling place.
When I go canvassing, I still find a lot of people who don’t even know when the primary day is—so please remind your friends and neighbors.
This is going to be a low-turnout primary, so your vote will have a bigger impact than ever.
If you need a reminder of why to vote for _me_ , I’ll direct you to a [candidate survey](https://cardinalnews.org/how-to-vote-in-louisa-county/#/us-house-5th-district-democratic/5th-district-democrats/topic/other-issues) I filled out for _Cardinal News_ , a Central and Southside Virginia news website. I’ll share my first answer up here, since it gives the main reason I’m running, then you can check out the rest of my replies below.
**“What's the biggest challenge facing the United States and how would you propose to address it?** “The US faces many problems right now—a war, rising cost of living, violations of civil rights, and so on. But they all have one cause: Donald Trump is asserting unlimited presidential power, going far beyond constitutional limits, and that's what is driving all the other problems.
“ Take the war in Iran, which he started without permission from Congress. If he had gone to Congress, they might haves asked about his strategy and whether he had one, and the costs of the war, and what could go wrong. It's clear by now he had no answers to those questions—and we're all paying the price at the gas pump and on the farms in the Fifth District.
“But the problem isn't just Trump, it's that congressmen like John McGuire are just rubber stamps. That's why I'm running. Congress has enormous power, and we need a member of Congress who will act like it and really represent the interests of people in this district instead of the interests of one guy at Mar-a-Lago.”
If you like what I’m saying, you can make a difference by voting for me, by encouraging your friends and neighbors to vote today, and by supporting my campaign.

---
| [DONATE TO HELP ME GET THIS IMPORTANT MESSAGE OUT](https://secure.actblue.com/donate/rob-tracinski-1)
---
| |

### What Do I Stand For?

It seems I was the only Democratic candidate to answer the [_Cardinal News_ survey](https://cardinalnews.org/how-to-vote-in-louisa-county/#/us-house-5th-district-democratic/5th-district-democrats/topic/biggest-challenge-us), which is a shame, because I put some thought into this and gave some interesting and fairly in-depth responses. So I’ll reproduce the survey and my answers here, so you can see where I stand—and also that I have a wider and more substantive set of policy positions than any other candidate in this race, of either party.
**What's the biggest challenge facing your district (or in the case of Senate candidate, the state) and how would you propose to address it?**
We have two big challenges, representing the character of this district, which is home to a world-class university, UVA, but also a heavily agricultural district. Both of those are being hit.

UVA has been struggling to maintain its academic independence, and it is an important center for scientific research, which has suffered from Trump's vandalism of science funding. At the same time, farmers in the rural parts of the district are getting hit hard by rising fuel and fertilizer prices, and Trump's trade war has restricted global markets for their crops.
Both of these are just a part of our big national crisis. Our district faces these challenges because the president has asserted unchecked power to declare war, impose tariffs, and make arbitrary decisions about spending. These are things that are supposed to be under the control of Congress, but our current Congress isn't doing its job and isn't standing up for their constituents.
**How would you assess the impact of HR 1, aka the One Big Beautiful Bill?**
HR 1 is a perfect example of how this Congress just acts as a rubber stamp for Donald Trump. It cut funding for all sorts of programs that benefit ordinary people in this district, from health care funding to food assistance, but it still did nothing to cut federal spending because it directed billions of dollars for ICE to send masked goons into our communities and ask people for their papers and to build massive detention centers where people with no criminal records are being held in notoriously inhumane conditions.

That is typical of this administration and its enablers in Congress. There's always money for programs designed to hurt people and never money for programs designed to help.
**What are your views on how Americans can better afford health care? Would you support the so-called "Medicare for All"? Why or why not?**
As a former Tea Party guy, I am very aware that Republicans have been promising for 16 years to "repeal and replace" Obamacare and propose something better, and somehow they never get around to it.

I support restoring the health care funding cut by HR1 to help put the system back together. And then I favor incremental reforms to lower costs and fix some of the perverse incentives built into the system as it is.

I don't support "Medicare for All," because I'm not convinced that will fix the actual problems. Even under Medicare as we have it now, we have dozens of rules that raise costs, limit access, and distort the system, and I favor incremental reforms to fix those problems.

Making heath care more affordable also requires standing up to the current anti-immigrant hysteria. We need immigrants for many different reasons, including as health-care workers. We can write all the government checks we want for health care, but it won't help us when we have a shortage of doctors and nurses, which is where we're heading—and anti-immigration policies are making that worse. We can see a warning of that in Britain, where a MAGA-style crackdown on immigration is endangering their national health care system. And contrary to claims made by Republicans, it is well documented that immigrants pay more into the American welfare system than they take out of it. Immigrants are helping pay for government benefits, and maybe we shouldn't be discouraging that.
**Up to 10 rural hospitals in Virginia have been listed as endangered. What would you propose to make sure they stay open?**
We need to restore the funding cut by HR1, but then also look at how we can adjust reimbursement rules to make sure rural hospitals remain viable.
**What are your views on immigration? Does the U.S. need more immigrants or fewer? What should be the criteria for entry and deportation? Under what circumstances should undocumented immigrants already here be given a pathway to citizenship?**
Donald Trump's anti-immigration policies are waking a lot of people up to the reality of immigration, because they show how his mass deportations are based on lies. He said he was going to target criminals and people who were violating the rules, but the majority of the people he has rounded up have no criminal records, and many were detained when they showed up for regular check-ins, precisely because they were trying to follow the rules. And many of them were loved and valued as members of their communities.

Trump's policies are shaped by hatred and xenophobia. They are not a reasonable response to legitimate concerns. There have been numerous studies showing that immigrants come here to work and contribute to our society, that they commit crimes at lower rates than the native born, and that they pay more into our welfare systems in taxes than they take out.

We've had previous anti-immigration hysterias in which demagogues vilified people with names like McGuire and names like Tracinski, and instead those people helped build this country and became as American as anybody else. We should clear the way for productive and law-abiding people to stay here, and immigration enforcement should go back to focusing on deporting dangerous criminals, not ordinary people who are just trying to make a better life for themselves and their families.

We should have more of an Ellis Island-style approach to immigration and oppose any policy that would have rejected our own grandparents or great-grandparents.
**Would you support an arms embargo on Israel? Why or why not? What else should we know about your views on Israel and Gaza?**
Decades ago, an Israeli friend warned me about Binyamin Netanyahu, pointing out that he presented two faces to the world. He came to America and in English said reasonable-sounding things about fighting terrorism—then he would go back to Israel and in Hebrew say things that supported the fanatical settler movement and its goal of ethnic cleansing against the Palestinians. That is exactly what has been playing out in his response to the October 7 terrorist attacks.
Israel has a right to exist, and I have no sympathy for terrorist organizations like Hamas and Hezbollah, which are highly repressive toward their own people and have their own murderous agenda. But that doesn't mean giving Netanyahu a blank check for a war that seems to have no strategy except as an excuse to kill Palestinians.
America has often been able to support Israel's legitimate claims while also using our support as leverage and not just a rubber stamp. We can do that again.
**What, if any, aid should the United States be supplying to Ukraine? Why or why not? What are the consequences if Russia succeeds in militarily claiming part of Ukraine?**
Full support for Ukraine—particularly air defense weapons and precision long-range artillery—is in American interests for three reasons.

First, Russian aggression against Ukraine threatens to return the world to the law of the jungle, a free-for-all in which the strong simply impose themselves on the weak. If Russia succeeds, we will face many more conflicts around the world than we do now. Every penny spent in Ukraine saves us dollars of future defense spending to deal with a more dangerous world.

Second, we owe Ukraine our support because they're fighting for democracy. Vladimir Putin developed the model of modern authoritarianism. He used politically connected "oligarchs" to control the media at home, while trying to intimidate Russia's neighbors and use its military power to carve off territory for his own aggrandizement. We can already see that when this model succeeds, it inspires imitators. We should support Ukraine to help ensure that the authoritarian model is revealed as a failure, in the same way the Cold War showed the failure of totalitarian communism and discredited the old Soviet model.
Third, we should support Ukraine because even without our full support, they're already winning, and in the process they are transforming modern warfare. Ukraine has become the world's drone superpower, mastering the new technology through innovation and constant trial-and-error on the battlefield.
We should be deeply concerned that the US military is falling behind--and the current administration is more concerned with getting corrupt defense contracts for Donald Trump, Jr., than with really modernizing our military.
Ukraine doesn't need an alliance with us as badly as we need an alliance with Ukraine, to help us modernize our military and learn the lessons of the new era of drone warfare.
**What, if anything, should the federal government do to either encourage or discourage development of artificial intelligence? Please address data centers as part of this.**
As a writer, I was once on the "emerging technology" beat and had to sift through a lot of Silicon Valley hype. The people who are saying AI is going to take over the world and take all our jobs predicted this was all going to happen by five years ago, so I think we should take both the promises and the fear with a giant grain of salt.

My greater worry is that circular financing in the AI industry is creating a multi-trillion-dollar bubble, and when it bursts, it will drag the real economy down with it.
I'm trying to help people find the best way to address real concerns about data centers without becoming Luddites. Most of the data centers in Virginia weren't built for AI. They were built so we can shop online and stream movies from Netflix. But if tech companies want to pour trillion into building new data centers, they should be required to pay their own way by building up the power and water infrastructure they need without pushing the costs onto consumers.
**President Trump has tried to block development of offshore wind energy. Dominion Energy is building an offshore wind facility off the coast of Virginia Beach and has long-range plans for more. What should the federal government's posture on offshore wind be? And energy development in general?**
We can always use an abundance of cheap and reliable power to drive down costs both for businesses and consumers.

It's reasonable to require power companies to mitigate negative effects like runoff and pollution, but not to discourage all development. We need what some people are calling "a liberalism that builds," because liberalism needs to show it can provide prosperity and not put unnecessary roadblocks in the way of progress.

Yet for all its rhetoric about being pro-energy, it is the Trump administration that is putting up the biggest barriers, fighting a war against solar and wind energy. Congress needs to fix a system that puts a thumb on the scale for fossil fuels—not coincidentally, Trump's donors—while actively blocking new sources of energy.

In the last decade, the price of solar energy and battery storage has been falling rapidly, making solar a cheaper, more practical, and reliable source—and one that could shield us from Trump's self-inflicted chaos in the Middle East.
**How would you assess the impact of the tariffs that President Trump has imposed?**
Tariffs always impose higher costs at home while starting trade wars that choke off markets for our own products.
A tariff on steel might be good for the relatively small number of workers at steel mills. But it raises costs for the far larger number of companies who use steel. This is why, for all of Trump's talk about reviving American industry, manufacturing jobs are down since he took office.
Meanwhile, farmers in Virginia are paying the price, too, because the trade war has cut off overseas markets for their crops.
The Constitution clearly gives Congress the power to set tariffs, yet Trump has declared that he can raise and lower them any time he likes. The courts have ruled these tariffs to be unconstitutional, but he keeps trying to find ways around the Constitution. This doesn't just damage our constitutional system. It also creates enormous economic uncertainty, so no one can plan ahead.
Congress needs to take back this power and stop the chaos.
**How would you assess the performance of President Trump? What actions would you take to support or oppose his agenda? For Democrats: Would you support impeachment? Why or why not?**
Trump has been a disaster. The economy isn't stronger, prices are higher, the American people are less safe from their own government, foreign dictators are emboldened, and Trump's war in the Middle East has left Iran in a stronger position than it was before.

Trump has only been effective at one thing: knocking down checks on his power, intimidating Republican in Congress into irrelevance, and centralizing all power in one person. But that is exactly the wrong thing.

Democrats in Congress should pass new laws to limit executive power and protect our constitutional rights—for example, stopping the FCC from threatening broadcast licenses. They should use Congress's control over spending as leverage to reassert its power.
Even if impeachment cannot remove Trump or his officials from office, the House should still attempt it just to bring his abuses of power to the attention of the American people and show that we do not accept the way he is changing our system of government.
**What changes, if any, to federal law would you like to see on abortion/contraception?**
We need a national law creating a reasonable minimum guarantee for reproductive rights.
The draconian abortion bans in Texas and elsewhere have demonstrated why overturning these protections was a mistake. Republican-controlled states have imposed laws that deny health care to pregnant women by making doctors, nurses, and hospitals afraid to deal with any serious complications. Women have suffered serious health problems, lost their fertility, and even died as a result.
Anyone who has had kids knows there are a lot of things that can go wrong in a pregnancy. Mothers, their spouses, and their doctors need to be able to make decisions based on the medical facts, not on the fear of being second-guessed by an overzealous prosecutor. Congress should pass a national protection for abortion rights that overrides these unnecessary and destructive state laws.
**What legislation, if any, would you support regarding firearms?**
I have made a promise to my friends and neighbors not to vote for any law that would make them or me a felon, which rules out the most radical gun-control proposals.

But also, the gun debate has evolved. At the height of the crime wave in the late 20th Century, the debate was about crime. Some thought we could stop violent crime by banning guns. Others argued that we needed the guns precisely to protect ourselves from crime.

Today, crime is back down to historically low levels, and many more of the deaths from firearms are a result of mental health struggles—suicides, especially among veterans, and school shootings. We should respond by focusing on more support for mental health while at the same time keeping guns out of the hands of unstable people.
**What else should voters know about you?**
I am not a traditional Democrat—15 to 20 years ago, I was active in the Tea Party movement in Charlottesville. I won't be down-the-line on every issue—which perhaps makes me a better fit for the Fifth District. Democrats here have a tendency to nominate candidates from the left-leaning Charlottesville area who have a hard time connecting with voters outside Albemarle County. I think I have an opportunity to change that, precisely because I'm not a traditional Democrat.

I signed up for the Democratic Party because of the "democracy" part, and I think that's something that can unify people across the district. I don't view this as a partisan campaign, but as a campaign for good old-fashioned Americanism and restoring the constitutional balance of powers.
I think I can even convince some conservatives--maybe a few of my old Tea Party friends--that they will really want more limitations on presidential power once they face the prospect of seeing someone they don't like in the White House.

clean_body: Remember to vote in the Fifth District Democratic Primary today. | | | | | | | | | | | | | Turn Out on Tuesday | | | | | | | | | | | | If you haven’t already voted early in the Fifth District Democratic primary, remember to turn out today for in-person voting at your local polling place. When I go canvassing, I still find a lot of people who don’t even know when the primary day is—so please remind your friends and neighbors. This is going to be a low-turnout primary, so your vote will have a bigger impact than ever. If you need a reminder of why to vote for me , I’ll direct you to a I filled out for Cardinal News , a Central and Southside Virginia news website. I’ll share my first answer up here, since it gives the main reason I’m running, then you can check out the rest of my replies below. “What's the biggest challenge facing the United States and how would you propose to address it? “The US faces many problems right now—a war, rising cost of living, violations of civil rights, and so on. But they all have one cause: Donald Trump is asserting unlimited presidential power, going far beyond constitutional limits, and that's what is driving all the other problems. “ Take the war in Iran, which he started without permission from Congress. If he had gone to Congress, they might haves asked about his strategy and whether he had one, and the costs of the war, and what could go wrong. It's clear by now he had no answers to those questions—and we're all paying the price at the gas pump and on the farms in the Fifth District. “But the problem isn't just Trump, it's that congressmen like John McGuire are just rubber stamps. That's why I'm running. Congress has enormous power, and we need a member of Congress who will act like it and really represent the interests of people in this district instead of the interests of one guy at Mar-a-Lago.” If you like what I’m saying, you can make a difference by voting for me, by encouraging your friends and neighbors to vote today, and by supporting my campaign. | | | What Do I Stand For? It seems I was the only Democratic candidate to answer the , which is a shame, because I put some thought into this and gave some interesting and fairly in-depth responses. So I’ll reproduce the survey and my answers here, so you can see where I stand—and also that I have a wider and more substantive set of policy positions than any other candidate in this race, of either party. What's the biggest challenge facing your district (or in the case of Senate candidate, the state) and how would you propose to address it? We have two big challenges, representing the character of this district, which is home to a world-class university, UVA, but also a heavily agricultural district. Both of those are being hit. UVA has been struggling to maintain its academic independence, and it is an important center for scientific research, which has suffered from Trump's vandalism of science funding. At the same time, farmers in the rural parts of the district are getting hit hard by rising fuel and fertilizer prices, and Trump's trade war has restricted global markets for their crops. Both of these are just a part of our big national crisis. Our district faces these challenges because the president has asserted unchecked power to declare war, impose tariffs, and make arbitrary decisions about spending. These are things that are supposed to be under the control of Congress, but our current Congress isn't doing its job and isn't standing up for their constituents. How would you assess the impact of HR 1, aka the One Big Beautiful Bill? HR 1 is a perfect example of how this Congress just acts as a rubber stamp for Donald Trump. It cut funding for all sorts of programs that benefit ordinary people in this district, from health care funding to food assistance, but it still did nothing to cut federal spending because it directed billions of dollars for ICE to send masked goons into our communities and ask people for their papers and to build massive detention centers where people with no criminal records are being held in notoriously inhumane conditions. That is typical of this administration and its enablers in Congress. There's always money for programs designed to hurt people and never money for programs designed to help. What are your views on how Americans can better afford health care? Would you support the so-called "Medicare for All"? Why or why not? As a former Tea Party guy, I am very aware that Republicans have been promising for 16 years to "repeal and replace" Obamacare and propose something better, and somehow they never get around to it. I support restoring the health care funding cut by HR1 to help put the system back together. And then I favor incremental reforms to lower costs and fix some of the perverse incentives built into the system as it is. I don't support "Medicare for All," because I'm not convinced that will fix the actual problems. Even under Medicare as we have it now, we have dozens of rules that raise costs, limit access, and distort the system, and I favor incremental reforms to fix those problems. Making heath care more affordable also requires standing up to the current anti-immigrant hysteria. We need immigrants for many different reasons, including as health-care workers. We can write all the government checks we want for health care, but it won't help us when we have a shortage of doctors and nurses, which is where we're heading—and anti-immigration policies are making that worse. We can see a warning of that in Britain, where a MAGA-style crackdown on immigration is endangering their national health care system. And contrary to claims made by Republicans, it is well documented that immigrants pay more into the American welfare system than they take out of it. Immigrants are helping pay for government benefits, and maybe we shouldn't be discouraging that. Up to 10 rural hospitals in Virginia have been listed as endangered. What would you propose to make sure they stay open? We need to restore the funding cut by HR1, but then also look at how we can adjust reimbursement rules to make sure rural hospitals remain viable. What are your views on immigration? Does the U.S. need more immigrants or fewer? What should be the criteria for entry and deportation? Under what circumstances should undocumented immigrants already here be given a pathway to citizenship? Donald Trump's anti-immigration policies are waking a lot of people up to the reality of immigration, because they show how his mass deportations are based on lies. He said he was going to target criminals and people who were violating the rules, but the majority of the people he has rounded up have no criminal records, and many were detained when they showed up for regular check-ins, precisely because they were trying to follow the rules. And many of them were loved and valued as members of their communities. Trump's policies are shaped by hatred and xenophobia. They are not a reasonable response to legitimate concerns. There have been numerous studies showing that immigrants come here to work and contribute to our society, that they commit crimes at lower rates than the native born, and that they pay more into our welfare systems in taxes than they take out. We've had previous anti-immigration hysterias in which demagogues vilified people with names like McGuire and names like Tracinski, and instead those people helped build this country and became as American as anybody else. We should clear the way for productive and law-abiding people to stay here, and immigration enforcement should go back to focusing on deporting dangerous criminals, not ordinary people who are just trying to make a better life for themselves and their families. We should have more of an Ellis Island-style approach to immigration and oppose any policy that would have rejected our own grandparents or great-grandparents. Would you support an arms embargo on Israel? Why or why not? What else should we know about your views on Israel and Gaza? Decades ago, an Israeli friend warned me about Binyamin Netanyahu, pointing out that he presented two faces to the world. He came to America and in English said reasonable-sounding things about fighting terrorism—then he would go back to Israel and in Hebrew say things that supported the fanatical settler movement and its goal of ethnic cleansing against the Palestinians. That is exactly what has been playing out in his response to the October 7 terrorist attacks. Israel has a right to exist, and I have no sympathy for terrorist organizations like Hamas and Hezbollah, which are highly repressive toward their own people and have their own murderous agenda. But that doesn't mean giving Netanyahu a blank check for a war that seems to have no strategy except as an excuse to kill Palestinians. America has often been able to support Israel's legitimate claims while also using our support as leverage and not just a rubber stamp. We can do that again. What, if any, aid should the United States be supplying to Ukraine? Why or why not? What are the consequences if Russia succeeds in militarily claiming part of Ukraine? Full support for Ukraine—particularly air defense weapons and precision long-range artillery—is in American interests for three reasons. First, Russian aggression against Ukraine threatens to return the world to the law of the jungle, a free-for-all in which the strong simply impose themselves on the weak. If Russia succeeds, we will face many more conflicts around the world than we do now. Every penny spent in Ukraine saves us dollars of future defense spending to deal with a more dangerous world. Second, we owe Ukraine our support because they're fighting for democracy. Vladimir Putin developed the model of modern authoritarianism. He used politically connected "oligarchs" to control the media at home, while trying to intimidate Russia's neighbors and use its military power to carve off territory for his own aggrandizement. We can already see that when this model succeeds, it inspires imitators. We should support Ukraine to help ensure that the authoritarian model is revealed as a failure, in the same way the Cold War showed the failure of totalitarian communism and discredited the old Soviet model. Third, we should support Ukraine because even without our full support, they're already winning, and in the process they are transforming modern warfare. Ukraine has become the world's drone superpower, mastering the new technology through innovation and constant trial-and-error on the battlefield. We should be deeply concerned that the US military is falling behind--and the current administration is more concerned with getting corrupt defense contracts for Donald Trump, Jr., than with really modernizing our military. Ukraine doesn't need an alliance with us as badly as we need an alliance with Ukraine, to help us modernize our military and learn the lessons of the new era of drone warfare. What, if anything, should the federal government do to either encourage or discourage development of artificial intelligence? Please address data centers as part of this. As a writer, I was once on the "emerging technology" beat and had to sift through a lot of Silicon Valley hype. The people who are saying AI is going to take over the world and take all our jobs predicted this was all going to happen by five years ago, so I think we should take both the promises and the fear with a giant grain of salt. My greater worry is that circular financing in the AI industry is creating a multi-trillion-dollar bubble, and when it bursts, it will drag the real economy down with it. I'm trying to help people find the best way to address real concerns about data centers without becoming Luddites. Most of the data centers in Virginia weren't built for AI. They were built so we can shop online and stream movies from Netflix. But if tech companies want to pour trillion into building new data centers, they should be required to pay their own way by building up the power and water infrastructure they need without pushing the costs onto consumers. President Trump has tried to block development of offshore wind energy. Dominion Energy is building an offshore wind facility off the coast of Virginia Beach and has long-range plans for more. What should the federal government's posture on offshore wind be? And energy development in general? We can always use an abundance of cheap and reliable power to drive down costs both for businesses and consumers. It's reasonable to require power companies to mitigate negative effects like runoff and pollution, but not to discourage all development. We need what some people are calling "a liberalism that builds," because liberalism needs to show it can provide prosperity and not put unnecessary roadblocks in the way of progress. Yet for all its rhetoric about being pro-energy, it is the Trump administration that is putting up the biggest barriers, fighting a war against solar and wind energy. Congress needs to fix a system that puts a thumb on the scale for fossil fuels—not coincidentally, Trump's donors—while actively blocking new sources of energy. In the last decade, the price of solar energy and battery storage has been falling rapidly, making solar a cheaper, more practical, and reliable source—and one that could shield us from Trump's self-inflicted chaos in the Middle East. How would you assess the impact of the tariffs that President Trump has imposed? Tariffs always impose higher costs at home while starting trade wars that choke off markets for our own products. Meanwhile, farmers in Virginia are paying the price, too, because the trade war has cut off overseas markets for their crops. His letter to the Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT requires developers to [disclose tax breaks](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkLFuhDAQRL_GdEa28R1c4SIN3aVNidbsAlYMRvbmOP4-Ir-QZqqnmdH7eg5PCDFs8yes5Pg9pWGjo0Ripjx8wzln2GbKGKiUcUkpliXt-2CUuUvVSWUHhBDPwVbovMKHrsjptrt1VjdtUy0OpxFGbb1v2pv2oBAfWiOg7TwZO6kquKtMdcpqrcxN18b6VisC8kajgUZYRRg45ZoXYnpDmeKZXpTrMa1VdAvzXkTzIUwvTH8cRz2FXBgiZW4vRpj-mhCmV90VjTA9eJ-YZcpIuUhaKc-0jaeEHwxcJMQod9owbLNEYJAjbXyRhYHpCEjC9FV2uB8hxlDurbBqXiHEv1P8P5UvZ34DAAD__yOGiiQ), power and water use, cooling technology, ownership, and noise and light controls. **Experts say that Democrats have no shot at flipping the U.S. Senate without winning in North Carolina.** This is one of the most important Senate races in the country, and like all elections in this critical swing state, it’s going to be decided by a razor-thin margin.
